html:
The Battles of Lexington and Concord were fought on 19 April 1775 in Massachusetts, in today's United States. Colonial militia drove a British column back to Boston. They were the first fights of the American Revolutionary War.

After years of quarrels over taxes and rights, Massachusetts was close to revolt. The British general Thomas Gage sent about 700 soldiers from Boston by night to seize militia weapons stored at Concord. Riders, among them Paul Revere, warned the countryside. At dawn in Lexington the soldiers met about 77 militiamen on the village green. Someone fired, nobody knows who, and eight militiamen were killed. At Concord's North Bridge the militia fired back and the British turned for home. Along the road thousands of militiamen shot at them from behind walls and trees. The British lost about 270 men killed, wounded or missing, and the colonists about 95.

The militia then surrounded Boston. In June the Thirteen Colonies formed an army under George Washington, and a year later came the Declaration of Independence. The poet Emerson later called the first shot at Concord "the shot heard round the world".
